# Design Lab: Metrics Collection, Storage, and Alerting

Instrumenting a Go application is one piece of a monitoring system. This lab connects the [metrics chapter](162-metrics-prometheus-design.qmd) to scraping, time-series storage, rule evaluation, and notification delivery. Use a local Go target and Prometheus; building a new time-series database is a separate experiment.

## Define the signal contract

Expose request counts, latency histograms, in-flight work, queue depth, oldest queued age, and dependency failures. Use bounded route and outcome labels; never use request IDs, email addresses, or raw URLs as metric labels. The [Prometheus instrumentation guidance](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/instrumentation/) explains the tradeoff between useful dimensions and cardinality.

Estimate series before deployment. Fifty instances × ten routes × five status classes creates 2,500 counter series. Ten finite classic histogram buckets plus `+Inf`, sum, and count add thirteen series per otherwise identical label set. At a 15-second scrape interval, 2,500 series alone produce about 14.4 million samples per day. Storage cost also depends on encoding, indexes, retention, and replica policy; do not multiply samples by a guessed raw struct size and call it disk capacity.

## Build the local system

1. Add a `prometheus.Registry` and `promhttp.HandlerFor` to the Go target using `github.com/prometheus/client_golang`. Commit the selected dependency versions in the exercise module's `go.mod` and `go.sum`.
2. Run a local Prometheus scraping the target every 15 seconds. Configure explicit retention and a bounded disk budget.
3. Generate normal traffic and synthetic failures through separate routes. Reuse a single target label such as `job="go-design-lab"` for this fixture.
4. Create one recording rule for traffic/error rate and one alert. Validate rule syntax and fixtures with `promtool check rules` and `promtool test rules`.
5. Send alerts to a fake receiver or local Alertmanager. Exercise grouping, deduplication, silencing, and resolved notifications.

A starting alert-rule fragment for the classic counter is:

```yaml
- alert: GoLabHighErrorRatio
  expr: |
    (
      sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="go-design-lab",status=~"5.."}[5m]))
      /
      clamp_min(sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="go-design-lab"}[5m])), 1)
    ) > 0.05
  for: 5m
  labels:
    severity: warning
  annotations:
    summary: "Go design lab has sustained server errors"
```

This is a lab threshold, not a universal SLO. Include a complete surrounding `groups` structure in the rule file. With a one-request/s denominator floor, low-traffic behavior is deliberately conservative; test it. A separate `up == 0` alert detects scrape failure because a failed scrape must not look like zero application errors. Monitor the monitoring system through an independent path.

## Storage and availability decisions

Scraping gives timestamped observations, not a lossless event log. A counter can increase between scrapes, and a restarted target can reset it. Apply rate functions before summing instance counters so resets are handled per series.

For a high-availability milestone, run independent collectors and describe duplicate-series handling at the query/storage layer. Two collectors writing the same unlabeled series do not automatically create a correct HA system. Keep rule-evaluation and notification dedupe identities explicit.

## Acceptance evidence

Stop a target, reset its counter, introduce one high-cardinality label in a disposable fixture, and stop the alert receiver. Record scrape failures, series growth, alert transition times, and notification retries. Use synthetic rule tests to verify both firing and recovery; do not wait for every five-minute interval during unit tests.

The project passes when an application failure and a telemetry failure produce distinguishable signals, bounded labels survive traffic growth, and duplicate alert evaluations do not create uncontrolled notification floods. Continue with the [notification delivery lab](../99-projects/101-system-design/02-notification-delivery.qmd) to examine receiver retries.
